concepts.text: A product term with k literals in an n-variable function fixes k variables and leaves n − k free, so it covers 2^(n − k) minterms. When a standard SOP is expanded, overlapping terms share minterms and the overlap must be counted once (inclusion–exclusion): AB + C'D in four variables covers 4 + 4 − 1 = 7 minterms. The same rule applied to sum terms counts maxterms in a standard POS.

concepts.plainText: A term with k literals covers 2^(n - k) of the 2^n rows

concepts.text: Common mistakes with minterms and maxterms:
items: Using the minterm literal rule for a maxterm: row 101 gives M5 = A' + B + C', not A + B' + C.
Reading the index with the wrong most significant bit: A is the MSB of F(A, B, C), so A'BC is m3, not m6.
Writing F' as ΠM of the same indices as Σm(F); that is F again, not its complement.
Forgetting that a single literal feeding the output gate of a NAND-NAND or NOR-NOR circuit must be complemented.

concepts.text: For list conversions write out 0 to 2^n − 1 and strike the given indices: what remains is the other list. F and F' never share an index, and F' in Σm form uses exactly the indices of F in ΠM form.

formulas.plainText: Maxterm i is the complement of minterm i
n variables give 2^n minterms and 2^n maxterms
The maxterm list is the set of indices missing from the minterm list
AND-OR = NAND-NAND: AB + CD = NAND(NAND(A,B), NAND(C,D))
OR-AND = NOR-NOR: (A+B)(C+D) = NOR(NOR(A,B), NOR(C,D))

notes.text: The subscript of a minterm is the decimal value of the input combination where it is 1: m5 of F(A,B,C) is 101 = AB'C. The maxterm with the same subscript is its complement, M5 = A' + B + C'.
The literal rule flips between the two forms. Minterm: bit 1 gives the true variable. Maxterm: bit 0 gives the true variable. Writing M5 as A + B' + C (using the minterm rule) is the classic mistake.
Sum m and product M lists of one function are complementary: F = sum m(1,2,4,7) is the same function as F = product M(0,3,5,6), and F' = sum m(0,3,5,6).

formulas.title: Minterm and maxterm relation
formulas.plainText: M_i = (m_i)'
formulas.description: The maxterm with index i is the complement of the minterm with the same index; each singles out row i of the truth table.

formulas.title: Number of minterms
formulas.plainText: 2^n minterms (and 2^n maxterms) for n variables
formulas.description: A function of n variables has 2^n possible minterms, one per truth-table row; a canonical SOP uses the subset where F = 1.

formulas.title: Minterm list to maxterm list
formulas.plainText: F = sum m(S) = product M(all indices not in S)
formulas.description: The POS maxterm list contains exactly the indices missing from the SOP minterm list, so conversion is immediate.

formulas.title: AND-OR to NAND-NAND
formulas.plainText: AB + CD = NAND(NAND(A,B), NAND(C,D))
formulas.description: Double inversion between the two levels turns every AND-OR (SOP) circuit into an all-NAND circuit with identical wiring; OR-AND becomes NOR-NOR the same way.

flashcards.front: What is a minterm, and how many are there for a 4-variable function?
flashcards.back: A product term containing every variable exactly once (true or complemented) that is 1 for a single input combination. Four variables give 2^4 = 16 minterms.

flashcards.front: How do you write a maxterm from a truth-table row where F = 0?
flashcards.back: OR the variables together, taking each variable uncomplemented if its bit is 0 and complemented if its bit is 1. Row 101 gives M5 = A' + B + C'.

flashcards.front: Which single gate type implements any SOP expression in two levels, and which implements any POS?
flashcards.back: SOP maps to AND-OR, which becomes NAND-NAND; POS maps to OR-AND, which becomes NOR-NOR. The wiring is unchanged, only the gate types.

questions.questionText: If F(A,B,C) = sum m(1,2,4,7), the product-of-maxterms form of F is:
questions.explanation: F is 1 on rows 1, 2, 4, 7 and therefore 0 on rows 0, 3, 5, 6. The maxterm list contains the indices where F = 0, so F = product M(0,3,5,6).

questions.questionText: For a three-variable function F(A,B,C), the maxterm M5 is:
questions.explanation: M5 corresponds to ABC = 101 and must be 0 on that row, so each variable is written uncomplemented when its bit is 0 and complemented when its bit is 1: A' + B + C'. AB'C is the minterm m5, its complement.

questions.questionText: A two-level AND-OR circuit that implements a sum-of-products expression can be replaced, without changing the wiring, by a circuit built only from:
options: OR gates followed by one AND gate
questions.explanation: Adding two inversions between the levels leaves the function unchanged, and by De Morgan an OR gate with inverted inputs is a NAND gate; so AND-OR becomes NAND-NAND. OR-AND (POS) is the form that converts to NOR-NOR.

questions.questionText: The standard SOP expression F = A + B'C, treated as a function of three variables, expands to a canonical SOP containing how many minterms?
questions.explanation: A alone covers the four minterms with A = 1 (m4, m5, m6, m7) and B'C covers m1 and m5. Since m5 is shared, F = sum m(1,4,5,6,7), five minterms.

questions.questionText: For a three-variable function F(A, B, C), the minterm m6 is:
questions.explanation: 6 = 110 in binary, so A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. In a minterm a 1 bit gives the true variable and a 0 bit the complement: m6 = ABC'. A' + B' + C is the maxterm M6.

questions.questionText: How many minterms are possible for a function of five variables?
questions.explanation: Each minterm corresponds to one truth-table row, and n variables give 2^n rows: 2^5 = 32.

questions.questionText: A canonical sum-of-products expression is:
options: A sum of product terms in which every term contains each variable exactly once
Any OR of AND terms, whatever variables they contain
A product of sum terms each containing every variable
The sum of products with the fewest possible literals
questions.explanation: Canonical SOP is a sum of minterms: every product contains all n variables, true or complemented. An SOP whose terms omit variables is a standard form, and the minimal one is what simplification produces.

questions.questionText: Which of the following expressions is in product-of-sums (POS) form?
questions.explanation: POS is an AND of OR terms whose OR terms contain only literals; a single literal such as D' counts as a one-literal sum. A(B + CD) and (AB + C)(A + D) contain a product inside a sum, and AB + C is SOP.

questions.questionText: A minterm of n variables has the value 1 for:
options: Exactly half of the input combinations
Every combination with at least one input equal to 1
Exactly one of the 2^n input combinations
questions.explanation: A minterm ANDs every variable in true or complemented form, so it is 1 only on the single row that matches it. A maxterm is the opposite: 0 on exactly one row and 1 on all the others.

questions.questionText: For a three-variable function F(A, B, C), the maxterm M0 is:
questions.explanation: M0 must be 0 only for ABC = 000. In a maxterm a 0 bit gives the true variable, so M0 = A + B + C. A'B'C' is the minterm m0 and A' + B' + C' is M7.

questions.questionText: The canonical SOP expression of F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 3) is:
questions.explanation: m0 = 000 = A'B'C', m1 = 001 = A'B'C and m3 = 011 = A'BC. The third option complements every literal (it is Σm(5, 6, 7)).

questions.questionText: For a function F(A, B, C), the expression AB + A'BC' is:
questions.explanation: It is an OR of AND terms, so it is SOP. The term AB does not contain C, so the form is standard rather than canonical; only A'BC' is a minterm.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly relates the maxterm M_i to the minterm m_i with the same index?
options: M_i is the dual of m_i
M_i is the complement of m_i
M_i equals the minterm m(2^n − 1 − i)
questions.explanation: m_i is 1 only on row i and M_i is 0 only on row i, so M_i = (m_i)'. The dual of m_i (keeping literals) gives the maxterm with index 2^n − 1 − i, not M_i.

questions.questionText: A two-level NOR-NOR circuit directly implements a Boolean expression written in:
questions.explanation: An OR-AND (POS) circuit becomes NOR-NOR when two inversions are inserted between the levels, because an AND gate with inverted inputs is a NOR gate. SOP maps onto NAND-NAND.

questions.questionText: When writing the canonical POS form of a function from its truth table, which rows are used?
options: Only the rows with an even number of 1 inputs
questions.explanation: Each maxterm is 0 on exactly one row, so the product of the maxterms for the 0-rows is 0 exactly there and 1 elsewhere. The canonical SOP uses the rows where F = 1.

questions.questionText: A four-variable function has 6 minterms in its canonical SOP. How many maxterms does its canonical POS contain?
questions.explanation: Four variables give 2^4 = 16 rows; each row appears either in the minterm list or the maxterm list, so there are 16 − 6 = 10 maxterms.

questions.questionText: The function F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The sum of all 2^n minterms covers every row of the truth table, so F = 1 for every input.

questions.questionText: For a four-variable function F(A, B, C, D), the minterm m9 is:
questions.explanation: 9 = 1001, so A = 1, B = 0, C = 0, D = 1 and m9 = AB'C'D. A'BCD' is m6 (complemented literals), A' + B + C + D' is the maxterm M9, and A'B'C'D is m1.

questions.questionText: For n variables, the product of all 2^n maxterms is equal to:
questions.explanation: Each maxterm is 0 on one row, and together they cover every row, so their product is 0 everywhere. The sum of all minterms is the opposite, 1 everywhere.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 4, 5, 10, 15). The product-of-maxterms form of F is:
questions.explanation: The maxterm list is every index from 0 to 15 that is missing from the minterm list: 16 − 6 = 10 maxterms. The Σm form of those indices would be F', not F.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C) = ΠM(0, 3, 5). The complement F' written as a sum of minterms is:
questions.explanation: F is 0 on rows 0, 3 and 5, so F' is 1 on exactly those rows: F' = Σm(0, 3, 5). Σm(1, 2, 4, 6, 7) is F itself.

questions.questionText: The expression F(A, B, C) = AB' + C expanded to canonical SOP is:
questions.explanation: AB' covers A = 1, B = 0: m4 and m5. C covers every row with C = 1: m1, m3, m5, m7. The union (m5 counted once) is Σm(1, 3, 4, 5, 7).

questions.questionText: The expression F(A, B, C) = (A + B')(A' + C) in canonical POS form is:
questions.explanation: A + B' = 0 when A = 0, B = 1 (rows 2, 3); A' + C = 0 when A = 1, C = 0 (rows 4, 6). So F = ΠM(2, 3, 4, 6), equivalently Σm(0, 1, 5, 7).

questions.questionText: In a four-variable function F(A, B, C, D), how many minterms are covered by the product term AB'?
questions.explanation: A term with k literals leaves n − k variables free, so it covers 2^(n − k) minterms: 2^(4 − 2) = 4 (m8, m9, m10, m11).

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C) = AB + A'C is to be built as a two-level NAND-NAND circuit, with complemented inputs available. How many NAND gates are needed?
questions.explanation: One first-level NAND per product term (AB and A'C) plus one output NAND: 2 + 1 = 3 gates, the same count and wiring as the AND-OR circuit.

questions.questionText: When F = AB + C is implemented in NAND-NAND form, the single-literal term C must be connected to the output NAND gate as:
questions.explanation: The output NAND computes (X·Y)' = X' + Y'. For its second input to contribute C, that input must be C'; so F = ((AB)'·C')' = AB + C.

questions.questionText: A circuit computes Y = NOR( NOR(A, B'), NOR(B, C) ). Y is equal to:
questions.explanation: Y = [(A + B')' + (B + C)']' = (A + B')(B + C) by De Morgan. A NOR-NOR circuit therefore realises a POS expression with the same wiring as OR-AND.

questions.questionText: A circuit computes Y = NAND( NAND(A, B'), NAND(A', C) ). Y is equal to:
questions.explanation: Y = [(AB')'·(A'C)']' = AB' + A'C by De Morgan, so NAND-NAND realises the SOP whose product terms are the first-level gate inputs.

questions.questionText: The canonical POS form of the two-variable function F(A, B) = A ⊕ B is:
questions.explanation: XOR is 0 when A = B, i.e. on rows 00 and 11, so F = ΠM(0, 3) = (A + B)(A' + B'). Σm(0, 3) is the XNOR function.

questions.questionText: Which statement about canonical and standard forms is correct?
options: A canonical SOP always has fewer literals than a standard SOP of the same function
The canonical POS of a function lists the indices where F = 1
In a standard SOP every product term must contain every variable
A function has exactly one canonical SOP (apart from term order) but may have many standard SOP forms
questions.explanation: The canonical SOP is fixed by the set of 1-rows, so it is unique; standard forms drop variables and are not unique. Canonical forms have the most literals, and the POS lists the 0-rows.

questions.questionText: For F(A, B, C) = ΠM(1, 2, 6), which input combination ABC makes F = 0?
questions.explanation: F is 0 exactly on the rows listed in ΠM. ABC = 110 is row 6, so F = 0; rows 3 (011), 5 (101) and 0 (000) are not in the list, so F = 1 there.

questions.questionText: The SOP expression F(A, B, C) = AB + A'C can also be written in POS form as:
questions.explanation: Expand (A + C)(A' + B) = AA' + AB + A'C + BC = AB + A'C + BC, and BC is the consensus of AB and A'C, so it equals AB + A'C. (A + B)(A' + C) gives AC + A'B instead.

questions.questionText: The canonical SOP expression A'BC + AB'C' + ABC of F(A, B, C) is written in minterm list form as:
questions.explanation: Read each term as a binary number with A as the most significant bit: A'BC = 011 = 3, AB'C' = 100 = 4, ABC = 111 = 7. Σm(6, 1, 7) results from reading C as the MSB.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C) = Σm(2, 5, 6). The complement F' in product-of-maxterms form is:
questions.explanation: F' is 0 where F is 1, i.e. on rows 2, 5 and 6, so F' = ΠM(2, 5, 6). ΠM(0, 1, 3, 4, 7) is F itself.

questions.questionText: The expression F(A, B, C) = A(B + C) in canonical POS form is:
questions.explanation: F = 0 whenever A = 0 (rows 0 to 3) or whenever B = C = 0 (rows 0 and 4). The union is ΠM(0, 1, 2, 3, 4); equivalently F = Σm(5, 6, 7).

questions.questionText: A three-variable function F is 1 when exactly one of its inputs is 1. Its canonical POS form is:
questions.explanation: F = 1 on rows 001, 010, 100, i.e. F = Σm(1, 2, 4). The maxterms are the remaining indices: ΠM(0, 3, 5, 6, 7).

questions.questionText: The three-variable odd-parity function F = A ⊕ B ⊕ C in minterm list form is:
questions.explanation: F = 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1: 001, 010, 100, 111, i.e. m1, m2, m4, m7. Σm(0, 3, 5, 6) is the even-parity function and Σm(3, 5, 6, 7) is the majority function.

questions.questionText: Why are SOP expressions usually implemented as NAND-NAND rather than AND-OR circuits?
options: NAND-NAND reduces the number of product terms in the expression
NAND gates are the simplest and fastest gates in common logic families, and one gate type simplifies the design
NAND-NAND converts a standard SOP into canonical form
NAND-NAND removes the need to complement any single-literal term
questions.explanation: In CMOS and TTL a NAND needs fewer transistors and switches faster than AND or OR, and a single universal gate type simplifies building and stocking circuits. The function and the number of terms are unchanged, and single literals still need complementing.

questions.questionText: A four-variable function is 1 on 13 of its 16 truth-table rows. Which canonical form is shorter, and how many terms does it have?
questions.explanation: The canonical SOP needs one minterm per 1-row (13 terms), while the canonical POS needs one maxterm per 0-row: 16 − 13 = 3 terms.

questions.questionText: An AND-OR-INVERT (AOI) gate has its inputs grouped as (A, B) and (C, D). Its output is:
questions.explanation: An AOI gate ANDs each group, ORs the products and inverts the result, so it gives the complement of an SOP: (AB + CD)', which by De Morgan is (A' + B')(C' + D').

questions.questionText: For a four-variable function F(A, B, C, D), the maxterm M10 is:
questions.explanation: 10 = 1010, so A = 1, B = 0, C = 1, D = 0. In a maxterm a 1 bit gives the complemented variable: M10 = A' + B + C' + D. AB'CD' is the minterm m10.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a canonical POS expression for a function F(A, B, C)?
questions.explanation: Every sum term of a canonical POS must contain all three variables. (A + B)(A' + B + C) and (A + B + C)(B' + C) each have a term missing a variable, and ABC + A'BC' is a canonical SOP.

questions.questionText: A four-variable function is 1 on 11 rows of its truth table. Its canonical POS form contains how many maxterms and how many literals in total?
questions.explanation: The POS uses the 0-rows: 16 − 11 = 5 maxterms. Every canonical term contains all 4 variables, so the total is 5 × 4 = 20 literals.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15) is minimised and built as a two-level NAND-NAND circuit (complemented inputs available). How many gates and total gate inputs does it need?
questions.explanation: The minterms with B = D = 0 (0, 2, 8, 10) give B'D' and those with B = D = 1 (5, 7, 13, 15) give BD, so F = B'D' + BD. That needs two 2-input NANDs and one 2-input output NAND: 3 gates and 6 inputs.

questions.questionText: The function F(A, B, C) = (A + B'C)(B + C') in canonical POS form is:
questions.explanation: Evaluate each row: F = 1 only for ABC = 100, 110 and 111 (for 001 the first factor is 1 but B + C' = 0). So F = Σm(4, 6, 7) = ΠM(0, 1, 2, 3, 5).

questions.questionText: The standard SOP F(A, B, C, D) = AB + C'D expands to a canonical SOP with how many minterms?
questions.explanation: AB covers 2^(4−2) = 4 minterms and C'D covers 4; the minterm ABC'D belongs to both, so the total is 4 + 4 − 1 = 7.

questions.questionText: For three-variable functions, F1 = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7) and F2 = ΠM(0, 1, 2, 3). The product F1·F2 is:
questions.explanation: F2 is 0 on rows 0 to 3, so it is 1 on rows 4 to 7 (F2 = A), while F1 = C. The AND is 1 only where both are 1: rows 5 and 7, i.e. F1·F2 = AC = Σm(5, 7).

questions.questionText: A circuit has three first-level NOR gates, NOR(A, B), NOR(A', C) and NOR(B', C'), feeding one 3-input NOR gate. Its output in minterm form is:
questions.explanation: The NOR-NOR circuit realises (A + B)(A' + C)(B' + C'). Checking all rows, every factor is 1 only for ABC = 010 and 101, so the output is Σm(2, 5).

questions.questionText: The standard POS F(A, B, C, D) = (A + B)(C' + D) expands to a canonical POS with how many maxterms?
questions.explanation: A + B = 0 on the 4 rows with A = B = 0, and C' + D = 0 on the 4 rows with C = 1, D = 0. The row 0010 is in both sets, so there are 4 + 4 − 1 = 7 maxterms.

questions.questionText: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 6, 7). A minimal POS expression for F is:
questions.explanation: F = 1 when A = B (rows 00x and 11x), so F = A'B' + AB. Its 0-rows 2, 3, 4, 5 combine into (A + B') and (A' + B), giving F = (A + B')(A' + B); (A + B)(A' + B') is the XOR instead.

subtopics.title: Karnaugh Maps
subtopics.subtitle: Graphical minimisation: Gray-code cells, grouping rules, prime implicants and don't-cares

concepts.text: Map Structure

A Karnaugh map (K-map) is the truth table redrawn as a grid in which every cell holds one minterm: 2 variables give a 2 x 2 map, 3 variables a 2 x 4 map and 4 variables a 4 x 4 map (16 cells). Rows and columns are labelled in Gray code order 00, 01, 11, 10, so that any two physically adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable. Adjacency continues across the edges: the left and right columns are neighbours, as are the top and bottom rows, and in a 4-variable map the four corner cells are all mutually adjacent. Each cell of an n-variable map has exactly n neighbours. Grouping adjacent 1s eliminates the variables that change within the group, which is the algebraic combining theorem AB + AB' = A applied by eye.

4-variable map: cell numbers (minterm index)

  AB\CD   00   01   11   10
   00      0    1    3    2
   01      4    5    7    6
   11     12   13   15   14
   10      8    9   11   10

Note the column order 00,01,11,10 (Gray), not 00,01,10,11.
Cells 0,2,8,10 (corners) form one valid group of 4 = B'D'.
Grouping Rules
Rules for forming groups of 1s (for SOP):
items: Groups contain 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells, powers of two only; a group of 3, 6 or 12 is invalid.
Groups must be rectangular (or square); diagonal cells are not adjacent.
The map wraps around: edge cells are adjacent to the opposite edge, and the four corners form a group.
Make each group as LARGE as possible and use as FEW groups as possible; every 1 must be in at least one group.
Groups may overlap freely if that enlarges them, but a group whose 1s are all already covered by other groups is redundant and must be dropped.
Don't-care cells (X) may be included as 1 when they enlarge a group and ignored otherwise.

concepts.text: A group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables and yields a product term with n - k literals: in a 4-variable map a single cell gives a 4-literal minterm, a pair gives 3 literals, a group of 4 gives 2, a group of 8 gives 1 and a group of all 16 means F = 1. To read a group, keep only the variables that are constant across it, written true if the constant value is 1 and complemented if it is 0. The minimal SOP is the OR of the terms read from the chosen groups, one term per group.

concepts.latex: \text{group of } 2^k \text{ cells} \Rightarrow \text{term with } n - k \text{ literals}
concepts.plainText: group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables, leaving n - k literals

concepts.text: Prime and Essential Prime Implicants

An implicant is any product term that covers only 1-cells (or don't-cares), i.e. any valid group. A prime implicant (PI) is a group that cannot be enlarged without including a 0. An essential prime implicant is a PI that covers at least one 1-cell no other PI covers; it must appear in every minimal expression. The systematic procedure is: mark all prime implicants; select every essential one; then cover any remaining 1s with the smallest possible set of the other prime implicants. When that last choice can be made in more than one way the function has several equally minimal expressions, so a K-map answer is minimal but not necessarily unique.
Worked 4-Variable Example

F(A,B,C,D) = sum m(0,1,2,4,5,6,8,9,12,13)

  AB\CD   00   01   11   10
   00      1    1    0    1
   01      1    1    0    1
   11      1    1    0    0
   10      1    1    0    0

Group 1 (8 cells, columns 00 and 01, all rows): C'
Group 2 (4 cells, rows 00 and 01, columns 00 and 10, wraps): A'D'
Minimal SOP:  F = C' + A'D'

Zeros: 3,7,11,15 (column 11) and 10,14 (rows 10,11 of column 10)
Group of 0s, column 11 (C=1, D=1):     sum term (C' + D')
Group of 0s, cells 10,11,14,15 (A=1, C=1): sum term (A' + C')
Minimal POS:  F = (C' + D')(A' + C')
How the two answers are read:
items: Group 1 spans all values of A and B and both columns with C = 0, so only C is constant: the term is C'.
Group 2 uses the wrap-around between columns 00 and 10; A = 0 and D = 0 are constant, giving A'D'. Both groups are prime and essential.
For POS, group the 0s in the same way, then write each group as a sum term with every constant variable complemented: cells with C = 1, D = 1 give (C' + D'); cells with A = 1, C = 1 give (A' + C').
Check by expanding the POS: (C' + D')(A' + C') = A'C' + C' + A'D' + C'D' = C' + A'D', the same as the SOP.

concepts.text: Don't-Care Conditions

Some input combinations never occur (the codes 1010 to 1111 never reach a BCD circuit) or their output is irrelevant; these are marked X on the map and may be treated as 1 or 0, whichever gives larger groups. For F(A,B,C,D) = sum m(1,3,7) + d(11,15), taking both don't-cares as 1 turns the column CD = 11 into a group of 4 read as CD, and m1 pairs with m3 to give A'B'D, so F = CD + A'B'D instead of the three-term expression obtained without the don't-cares. Don't-cares are never required to be covered, so an X that does not enlarge a group is simply left out.
Limits and Beyond Four Variables

K-maps stay practical up to four variables. A 5-variable function is drawn as two 4-variable maps (one for E = 0, one for E = 1) stacked so that cells in the same position are adjacent, and 6 variables need four maps; beyond that the adjacencies are too hard to see. For larger problems, and for software, the Quine-McCluskey tabular method performs the same prime-implicant search algorithmically. Whatever the method, minimisation trades gates and inputs for a function that is logically identical to the original truth table.
Going Deeper: Karnaugh Maps

Why does a rectangle of 2^k cells always collapse to one product term? Two adjacent cells differ in one variable X, so their minterms are PX and PX', and PX + PX' = P. Two adjacent pairs that differ in a second variable Y combine again in the same way, so a block of 4 loses two variables and a block of 8 loses three. In the language of n-dimensional cubes, a valid group is a subcube: its cell numbers agree in n - k bit positions and take every combination in the other k. That is why a group must be a power of two in size and why an L-shape or a diagonal never works.

concepts.latex: P X + P \overline{X} = P \;\Rightarrow\; 2^k \text{ adjacent cells} \to 1 \text{ term}
concepts.plainText: PX + PX' = P, applied k times, merges 2^k adjacent cells into one product term

concepts.text: Worked Example: Prime Implicant Chart and a Redundant Group

F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(3,4,5,7,9,13,14,15)

  AB\CD  00  01  11  10
   00     0   0   1   0
   01     1   1   1   0
   11     0   1   1   1
   10     0   1   0   0

Prime implicants: A'BC' (4,5)  A'CD (3,7)  ABC (14,15)
                  AC'D (9,13)  BD (5,7,13,15)
Essential: m4 only in A'BC', m3 only in A'CD,
           m14 only in ABC,  m9 only in AC'D
The four EPIs already cover 5, 7, 13, 15, so BD is redundant.
F = A'BC' + A'CD + ABC + AC'D   (4 terms, 12 literals)

The centre square BD is the largest group on the map, and choosing it first is the classic mistake: it leaves m3, m4, m9 and m14 needing four more pairs, giving five terms. Always pick essential prime implicants first, then cover what is left. A useful habit is to start from 1-cells that have only one possible group (isolated or corner cells), because the group through such a cell is always essential.
Five-Variable Maps

F(A,B,C,D,E) = Σm(0,2,5,7,8,10,16,18,21,23,24,26)
Two 16-cell maps over BCDE: left A = 0 (m0-m15), right A = 1 (m16-m31)
Cells in the same position (m and m + 16) are adjacent.

A = 0 map 1s: 0,2,8,10 (corners) and 5,7
A = 1 map 1s: 16,18,24,26 (corners) and 21,23
Corners in both maps: 8 cells, C = 0 and E = 0 fixed  -> C'E'
5,7,21,23: B = 0, C = 1, E = 1 fixed                  -> B'CE
F = C'E' + B'CE

rows: Tabular: combine terms differing in one bit
Up to 4 variables, 5 or 6 with care
PI chart, then Petrick's method if cyclic
Included in the combining step, not in the chart
Long hand working for many minterms

concepts.text:
Quine–McCluskey for F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,2,3,5,7)
Group by count of 1s:  0: 000 | 1: 001, 010 | 2: 011, 101 | 3: 111
Pairs:  0,1 = 00-   0,2 = 0-0   1,3 = 0-1   1,5 = -01
        2,3 = 01-   3,7 = -11   5,7 = 1-1        (all ticked)
Quads:  0,1,2,3 = 0--  (A')     1,3,5,7 = --1  (C)
No further combination: prime implicants A' and C, both essential
F = A' + C

Hazards come from the same map. In a two-level SOP circuit, if two adjacent 1-cells are covered by different groups, a change of the one variable that separates them switches one AND gate off while the other switches on, and unequal delays can let the output dip to 0 (a static-1 hazard). The cure is to add the redundant group that bridges the two cells, which is the consensus term; for F = A'B + AC the hazard occurs with B = 1, C = 1 while A changes, and the bridging term is BC. POS circuits suffer the dual static-0 hazard, and a dynamic hazard (several bounces during one intended change) arises only in multi-level circuits.

Common K-map slips: labelling columns 00, 01, 10, 11 instead of Gray order; forgetting that the outer edges and the four corners wrap around; writing a group of 0s as a product instead of a sum with complemented constants; covering don't-cares that do not enlarge a group; and selecting the biggest group first instead of the essential ones, which can leave a redundant term in the answer.

formulas.plainText: An n-variable K-map has 2^n cells

formulas.latex: \text{group of } 2^k \Rightarrow k \text{ variables eliminated}, \; n - k \text{ literals}
formulas.plainText: Group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables and leaves n - k literals
Each cell in an n-variable map is adjacent to exactly n other cells
Combining theorem AB + AB' = A: why two adjacent 1s merge into one term
Group the 0s to get F' as SOP; complement it (De Morgan) to get F as POS

notes.text: Column/row order is Gray code (00, 01, 11, 10), NOT binary order. Writing 00, 01, 10, 11 destroys adjacency and gives wrong groupings.
Corners of a 4-variable map form a valid group of 4 (they are all mutually adjacent by wrap-around) and read as B'D'. Also, a group covering the whole map means F = 1.

Count literals to check your answer: in a 4-variable map a pair gives 3 literals, a group of 4 gives 2, a group of 8 gives 1. If a term you wrote has the wrong number of literals for its group size, re-read the group.

Don't-cares (X) are optional 1s: include them only when they enlarge a group, and never form a group made only of Xs. A K-map gives a minimal expression, but when non-essential prime implicants can be chosen in more than one way several equally minimal answers exist.

formulas.title: K-map size
formulas.plainText: cells = 2^n (2 vars: 4, 3 vars: 8, 4 vars: 16)
formulas.description: One cell per minterm; a 4-variable map is 4 x 4 and a 3-variable map is 2 x 4.

formulas.title: Variables eliminated by a group
formulas.plainText: Group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables, leaving n - k literals
formulas.description: A pair removes one variable, a group of 4 removes two, a group of 8 removes three; valid group sizes are powers of 2 only.

formulas.title: Adjacency count
formulas.plainText: each cell has n adjacent cells (with wrap-around)
formulas.description: In an n-variable map each cell differs in one variable from exactly n others, which is why the edges and corners wrap around.

formulas.title: POS from the zeros
formulas.plainText: Group the 0s to get F' in SOP, then complement with De Morgan to get F in POS
formulas.description: Each group of 0s becomes a sum term in which every constant variable is written complemented; the AND of those terms is the minimal POS.

flashcards.front: What are 'don't care' conditions in a K-map?
flashcards.back: Input combinations that never occur or whose output is irrelevant (marked X). They may be treated as 0 or 1, whichever gives larger groups and a simpler expression.

flashcards.front: What is an essential prime implicant?
flashcards.back: A prime implicant (a group that cannot be enlarged) that covers at least one 1-cell no other prime implicant covers. It must appear in every minimal expression.

flashcards.front: Which four cells of a 4-variable K-map form a group even though they are not visibly touching, and what term do they give?
flashcards.back: The four corner cells (minterms 0, 2, 8, 10). By wrap-around they are mutually adjacent and read as B'D'.

flashcards.front: How is a POS expression obtained from a K-map?
flashcards.back: Group the 0s instead of the 1s. Each group becomes a sum term with every constant variable complemented, and the terms are ANDed together.

questions.questionText: A two-variable K-map has 1s in cells m1, m2 and m3 (variables A, B). The minimal SOP expression is:
questions.explanation: Cells m1 and m3 form the column B = 1, giving B; m2 and m3 form the row A = 1, giving A. The overlapping pairs give F = A + B, the OR function.

questions.questionText: Simplify F(A,B,C) = Σm(1,3,5,7) using a K-map.
questions.explanation: The four 1s (001, 011, 101, 111) all have C = 1 while A and B take every value, so one group of four gives F = C.

questions.questionText: Simplify F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,4,5) using a K-map.
questions.explanation: m0, m1, m4 and m5 are 000, 001, 100 and 101: only B is constant (B = 0), so the group of four reads B'.

questions.questionText: The minimal SOP form of F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,2,5,7) is:
questions.explanation: m0 and m2 (A = 0, C = 0) pair to A'C'; m5 and m7 (A = 1, C = 1) pair to AC. F = A'C' + AC, which is the XNOR of A and C, not the XOR.

questions.questionText: A 4-variable K-map (A, B, C, D) has 1s only in m0, m2, m8 and m10. The simplified expression is:
questions.explanation: m0, m2, m8 and m10 are the four corner cells (0000, 0010, 1000, 1010). A and C vary while B = 0 and D = 0, so F = B'D'.

questions.questionText: Simplify F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1,3,9,11).
questions.explanation: The cells 0001, 0011, 1001 and 1011 keep B = 0 and D = 1 while A and C change; the group of four (wrapping top to bottom) gives B'D.

questions.questionText: In a 5-variable K-map, a valid group of 4 cells produces a product term with how many literals?
questions.explanation: A group of 2^k cells eliminates k variables. With n = 5 and k = 2 the term keeps 5 - 2 = 3 literals.

questions.questionText: How many cells does a 5-variable Karnaugh map contain?
questions.explanation: One cell per minterm: 2^5 = 32 cells, usually drawn as two 16-cell maps side by side.

questions.questionText: In a 4-variable K-map (A, B, C, D, with A the most significant bit), which cells are adjacent to cell m5?
questions.explanation: m5 = 0101. Changing one bit at a time gives 1101 = m13, 0001 = m1, 0111 = m7 and 0100 = m4; m6 (0110) differs from m5 in two bits.

questions.questionText: Which set of cells is NOT a valid group in a 4-variable K-map (A, B, C, D)?
questions.explanation: m0, m5, m10 and m15 lie on a diagonal; each differs from its neighbour in two variables, so they are not adjacent. The other sets are the corners (B'D'), B'D and BC', all valid groups of four.
m0, m1, m4, m5 have A = 0, C = 0 (group A'C'); m10, m11, m14, m15 have A = 1, C = 1 (group AC). F = A'C' + AC.

questions.questionText: The minimal SOP for F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,2,5,7,8,10,13,15) is:
questions.explanation: The corners 0, 2, 8, 10 give B'D' and the centre block 5, 7, 13, 15 gives BD, so F = BD + B'D' (B XNOR D).
The top two rows (m0 to m7) form a group of 8 = A'. m8 and m10 join m0 and m2 in the corner group B'D'. F = A' + B'D'.

questions.questionText: Find the minimal SOP of F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,1,2,5,8,9,10).
questions.explanation: Groups: m0, m1, m8, m9 give B'C'; the corners m0, m2, m8, m10 give B'D'; m1 and m5 give A'C'D. All three are essential, so F = B'C' + B'D' + A'C'D.

questions.questionText: Find the minimal POS of F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,1,2,5,8,9,10).
questions.explanation: Group the 0s: row AB = 11 gives AB, column CD = 11 gives CD, and m4, m6, m12, m14 give BD'. So F' = AB + CD + BD' and, by De Morgan, F = (A' + B')(C' + D')(B' + D).

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1,3,7,11,15) + d(0,2,5). Which of the following is a minimal SOP for F?
questions.explanation: CD covers m3, m7, m11, m15. m1 still needs a group: A'B' (using d0, d2) or A'D (using d5) both work with two literals, so CD + A'B' is minimal (CD + A'D is equally minimal). B'D, AD and A'C' each cover a 0-cell (m9 or m4).

questions.questionText: For F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1,3,7,11,15) + d(0,2,5), the minimal POS expression is:
questions.explanation: Grouping the 0s (with d0 and d2 taken as 0) gives D' (the eight cells with D = 0) and AC' (m8, m9, m12, m13). F' = D' + AC', so F = D(A' + C).

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,2,5,6,7). How many essential prime implicants does F have?
questions.explanation: Every 1-cell is covered by two prime implicants (A'B', A'C', B'C, BC', AB, AC form a ring of pairs), so no PI is essential. This is a cyclic function; a minimal cover still needs 3 of the 6 PIs, e.g. A'B' + BC' + AC.

questions.questionText: For F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1,5,6,7,11,12,13,15), the group BD (cells m5, m7, m13, m15) is:
options: Not a prime implicant, because it can be enlarged to a group of 8
Required, because m15 is covered by no other prime implicant
A prime implicant that is not needed in the minimal SOP
questions.explanation: The four essential PIs A'C'D, A'BC, ABC' and ACD already cover m5, m7, m13 and m15, so BD is a redundant prime implicant: F = A'C'D + A'BC + ABC' + ACD.

questions.questionText: A 5-variable K-map is drawn as two 16-cell maps, one for A = 0 (m0 to m15) and one for A = 1 (m16 to m31). Which cell of the A = 1 map is adjacent to m3?
questions.explanation: Cells in the same position of the two maps differ only in A, so m3 (00011) is adjacent to m3 + 16 = m19 (10011). m18, m27 and m17 each differ from m3 in two bits.

questions.questionText: Using a 5-variable K-map, simplify F(A,B,C,D,E) = Σm(0,2,4,6,9,13,21,23,25,29,31).
questions.explanation: m0, m2, m4, m6 give A'B'E'; m9, m13, m25, m29 (same positions in both maps) give BD'E; m21, m23, m29, m31 give ACE. All three are essential.

questions.questionText: A circuit with BCD input ABCD (A = MSB) must output 1 when the digit is 5 or more. Using the codes 1010 to 1111 as don't-cares, the minimal SOP is:
questions.explanation: 1s at m5 to m9, don't-cares at m10 to m15. The bottom two rows (with Xs) give A, m5, m7 with m13, m15 give BD, and m6, m7 with m14, m15 give BC. F = A + BD + BC.

questions.questionText: Simplify F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,4,8,12).
questions.explanation: The four cells form the column CD = 00 across all four rows. A and B vary, C = 0 and D = 0, so F = C'D'.

questions.questionText: A 4-variable K-map has 1s only in m5, m7, m13 and m15. The simplified function is:
questions.explanation: The cells 0101, 0111, 1101, 1111 form the centre square; B = 1 and D = 1 are constant, so F = BD.

questions.questionText: The minimal SOP of F(A,B,C) = Σm(1,2,3,5,7) is:
questions.explanation: m1, m3, m5, m7 form the group C. m2 pairs with m3 (A = 0, B = 1) to give A'B. F = C + A'B.

questions.questionText: When F(A,B,C,D) = A + B'C is plotted on a 4-variable K-map, how many cells contain 1?
questions.explanation: A covers the 8 cells with A = 1. B'C covers 4 cells, 2 of which (A = 1) are already counted, adding m2 and m3. Total = 8 + 2 = 10.

questions.questionText: On a 4-variable K-map (A, B, C, D), the product term AC' occupies how many cells?
questions.explanation: AC' fixes two of the four variables and leaves B and D free, so it covers 2^2 = 4 cells (m8, m9, m12, m13).

questions.questionText: The minimal POS of F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,2,3,6) is:
questions.explanation: The 0s are m4, m5, m7. m4 and m5 (A = 1, B = 0) give the sum term (A' + B); m5 and m7 (A = 1, C = 1) give (A' + C'). F = (A' + B)(A' + C').

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C,D) = ΠM(3,7,11,15). The minimal POS form is:
questions.explanation: The four 0s form the column CD = 11 (C = 1, D = 1). A group of 0s is written as a sum with each constant variable complemented, so F = (C' + D').

questions.questionText: For F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,1,2,3,4), grouping the 0-cells of the K-map gives the complement F' as:
questions.explanation: The 0s are m5, m6, m7. m6, m7 give AB and m5, m7 give AC, so F' = AB + AC (and F = A' + B'C').

questions.questionText: In the Quine–McCluskey method, combining the minterms m4 (0100) and m6 (0110) produces the term:
questions.explanation: The two codes differ only in the third bit (C), which is replaced by a dash: 01-0, i.e. A'BD'.

questions.questionText: In the first step of the Quine–McCluskey tabulation method, the minterms are arranged in groups according to:
options: The number of 1s in their binary representation
Their decimal value in ascending order
The number of variables that appear complemented in the final answer
The Gray-code position of each minterm on the K-map
questions.explanation: Only terms in neighbouring groups (1s count differing by one) can differ in a single bit, so grouping by the count of 1s limits the comparisons that must be made.

questions.questionText: Which pair of minterms can be combined in the first stage of the Quine–McCluskey method?
questions.explanation: m5 = 0101 and m7 = 0111 differ in exactly one bit, giving 01-1. 6/9 (0110/1001) differ in four bits, 2/4 in two bits and 3/12 in four bits.

questions.questionText: In a Quine–McCluskey table for a 4-variable function, the minterm m13 is placed in the group of terms containing:
questions.explanation: 13 = 1101 in binary, which contains three 1s.

questions.questionText: At the end of the Quine–McCluskey tabulation, the prime implicants are:
options: The terms produced in the final stage only
The original minterms of the first column
The terms that were combined the greatest number of times
The terms that were never combined (never ticked) at any stage
questions.explanation: A term that cannot be combined with any other differs from all of them in more than one bit, so it cannot be enlarged; every unticked term, from any column, is a prime implicant.

questions.questionText: The main advantage of the Quine–McCluskey method over the Karnaugh map is that it:
options: Always gives an expression with fewer literals than a K-map
Cannot use don't-care conditions, so it is simpler
Is a systematic procedure that can be programmed and used for many variables
questions.explanation: Both methods find the same minimal result; Quine–McCluskey replaces visual grouping with a table-driven algorithm, which suits computers and functions with more than four or five variables.

questions.questionText: In the second stage of the Quine–McCluskey method, which pair of terms can be combined?
questions.explanation: Two terms combine only if their dashes are in the same positions and they differ in exactly one other bit. 01-0 and 11-0 differ only in the first bit, giving -1-0 (BD'). The other pairs have dashes in different positions.

questions.questionText: A function whose prime implicant chart contains no essential prime implicant (every minterm is covered by at least two PIs) is called:
questions.explanation: In a cyclic chart no column has a single mark, so selection must be made by trial or by Petrick's method. Incompletely specified refers to don't-cares, which is a different idea.

questions.questionText: A static-1 hazard in a combinational circuit is:
options: A momentary 1 at the output when it should remain 0 during a single input change
Several output transitions when the output should change only once
An output permanently stuck at 1 because of a faulty gate
A momentary 0 at the output when it should remain 1 during a single input change
questions.explanation: Static-1 means the correct output is 1 before and after the change but a glitch to 0 appears because of unequal path delays. The first option describes a static-0 hazard and the second a dynamic hazard.

questions.questionText: F = AB' + BC has a static-1 hazard when A = 1, C = 1 and B changes. Which term must be added to remove it without changing the function?
questions.explanation: The consensus of AB' and BC (eliminating B) is AC. It covers both cells 101 and 111, so the output is held at 1 while B switches, and AB' + BC + AC equals AB' + BC.

questions.questionText: For the two-level SOP circuit F = A'C' + AB, a static-1 hazard can occur when:
questions.explanation: Cells 010 and 110 are both 1 but are covered by different terms (A'C' and AB), so when A switches one AND gate turns off as the other turns on. With B = 0, C = 0 the output really changes; in the other two cases a single term stays 1.

questions.questionText: In a two-level POS realisation, a static-0 hazard is removed by:
options: Adding a redundant product term that covers the adjacent 1-cells
Adding a redundant sum term that covers the pair of adjacent 0-cells
Replacing the OR gates by XOR gates
questions.explanation: POS is the dual of SOP: two adjacent 0-cells covered by different sum terms can glitch to 1, and the cure is the consensus sum term that covers both.

questions.questionText: Which statement about don't-care conditions in a K-map is NOT correct?
options: A don't-care may be treated as 1 or 0, whichever gives larger groups
In a BCD input circuit the codes 1010 to 1111 can be treated as don't-cares
Every don't-care cell must be covered by at least one group
A group made only of don't-cares adds an unnecessary term
questions.explanation: Don't-cares are optional: they are included only when they enlarge a group of 1s and are otherwise left uncovered.

questions.questionText: A prime implicant of a Boolean function is:
options: A term that must appear in every minimal expression
A product term whose group cannot be enlarged without including a 0-cell
A product term containing all n variables
questions.explanation: A prime implicant is a maximal group. A term that must appear in every minimal expression is an essential PI, and a term with all n variables is a minterm.

questions.questionText: In a 6-variable K-map, each cell is adjacent to how many other cells?
questions.explanation: Each cell is adjacent to the cells that differ from it in exactly one variable; with 6 variables there are 6 such cells.

questions.questionText: Find the minimal SOP of F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,1,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,14).
questions.explanation: Essential PIs: B'C' (m0, m1, m8, m9) and A'B (m4 to m7). m10 and m14 remain; the single group ACD' covers both. AB'D' misses m14, CD' includes the 0-cell m2, and A'C' leaves m8, m9 uncovered.
